text: In the last lesson you framed the churn problem, explored the data, sealed away a test set, and set a baseline of 0.5 ROC AUC. Now you build. This lesson creates a leakage-safe preprocessing pipeline, compares three models with cross-validation, tunes the most promising one, and reads what the winner learned. The result may surprise you — the fanciest model does not win.

Our features need different treatment — numeric columns need imputing and scaling, categorical columns need one-hot encoding. A ColumnTransformer applies the right steps to the right columns. Putting it inside a Pipeline with the model means every cross-validation fold learns its imputer, scaler, and encoder from that fold's training portion only — exactly how you avoid the leakage you studied earlier.

Comparing logistic regression, a shallow decision tree, and a random forest, each scored by 5-fold stratified cross-validation on the training set using ROC AUC: logistic regression leads with a mean AUC of 0.776, while both the tree and the untuned forest sit near 0.70. An untuned forest with fully grown trees overfits the training folds — the bias-variance trade-off from Chapter 1, showing up in real numbers.

Giving the forest a fair chance, searching a small grid over tree depth and minimum leaf size: the best settings are max_depth 3 and min_samples_leaf 1, with a cross-validated AUC of 0.749. Tuning helped the forest by about 0.05, but it still trails logistic regression's 0.776.

A quick sweep of logistic regression's own regularization strength, C, tells the same story — scores of 0.754, 0.774, 0.776, 0.776, 0.776 across five values, meaning the default C equals 1 is already sitting right on the plateau. Nothing left to gain there.

Why does the simple model win? Our synthetic data was generated with an additive, roughly linear signal — exactly the shape logistic regression assumes. On real data the answer isn't always this tidy, which is exactly why you compare models rather than assuming. We choose logistic regression as the final model — it scores best, trains instantly, and is easy to explain.

Reading the fitted coefficients: longer tenure, longer contracts, and autopay all reduce churn risk, with coefficients of negative 0.82, negative 1.07, negative 1.81, and negative 0.40. Higher monthly charges and more support calls raise it, at positive 0.39 and 0.38. This matches the exact patterns you found in lesson 27 — a good sanity check.

For comparison, the tuned forest's feature importances tell the same story a different way — tenure ranks first at 0.437, followed by the two-year contract flag at 0.245 and monthly charges at 0.145. To recap: you built one leakage-safe pipeline, compared three models with cross-validation, tuned the forest, and discovered the simple model was best. The test set is still sealed. In lesson 29, you evaluate the final model on it and package the project for your portfolio.
